To keep your plot, you must attend at least two of the four monthly work mornings, where members help clear paths and repair the shared tool shed. Plots that show no planting by May 15 will be offered to the next person on the waiting list. Hoses may be used only before 9 a.m. or after 6 p.m. to reduce water loss. text.title: The Invention of Paper in Han China
text.body:
Before paper existed, Chinese scribes wrote on strips of bamboo or on silk. Both materials had serious drawbacks. Bamboo strips were bulky and heavy, so a single long book could fill a cart, while silk was smooth and light but far too expensive for everyday records.

Chinese tradition credits a court official named Cai Lun with inventing paper in 105 CE. According to historical records, he pounded tree bark, hemp, old rags and worn fishing nets into a wet pulp, spread the pulp thinly over a screen, and let it dry into sheets. Archaeologists, however, have found fragments of paper in tombs that are older than Cai Lun, which suggests that he improved and promoted an existing technique rather than creating it from nothing.

Whatever its exact origins, the new material transformed record keeping. Because paper was cheap to produce from inexpensive materials, government offices could keep far more documents, and books became easier to copy and carry. Over the following centuries, papermaking spread to Korea and Japan and, much later, through the Islamic world to Europe.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 1, what was the main disadvantage of silk as a writing material?
options: It cost too much for ordinary records.
It was too heavy to carry easily.
It was too rough to write on clearly.
It could not be made into long books.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says silk was 'far too expensive for everyday records'.

questions.prompt: The word "promoted" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
options: moved to a higher rank
earned money from
kept secret from others
encouraged the use of
questions.explanation: Cai Lun 'improved and promoted an existing technique', meaning he encouraged its use.

questions.prompt: What does paragraph 2 suggest about Cai Lun?
options: He was the first person to write on paper.
He learned papermaking from archaeologists.
He was probably not the first to make paper.
He preferred bamboo strips to paper sheets.
questions.explanation: Paper fragments 'older than Cai Lun' suggest he improved an existing technique rather than inventing it.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 2, all of the following were used in Cai Lun's papermaking process EXCEPT
options: tree bark
bamboo strips
old rags
worn fishing nets
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 lists tree bark, hemp, old rags and fishing nets; bamboo strips appear only in paragraph 1 as an earlier writing surface.

questions.prompt: Why does the author mention that "a single long book could fill a cart"?
options: To show how heavy and bulky bamboo records were
To explain why silk was used for long books
To suggest that books were rare in Han China
To describe how scribes moved between offices
questions.explanation: The detail illustrates the claim that 'bamboo strips were bulky and heavy'.

text.title: How Camels Survive in the Desert
text.body:
Camels are famous for living in hot, dry places where few other large animals can survive. Many people believe that a camel's hump is full of water, but this is not true. The hump actually stores fat. When food is hard to find, the camel's body can break down this fat for energy.

Camels are also very good at saving water. They can go for a week or more without drinking, and when they finally reach water, they can drink up to 100 litres in about ten minutes. Their body temperature can rise by several degrees during the day, so they do not need to sweat as much as other animals.

Their bodies protect them from sand as well. Camels have two rows of long eyelashes, and they can close their nostrils during sandstorms. Their wide, flat feet also help them walk on soft sand without sinking. These features make the camel well suited to life in the desert.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says 'The hump actually stores fat'.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says camels 'can close their nostrils during sandstorms'.

questions.explanation: The author mentions the belief and then says 'this is not true', so the purpose is to correct it.

text.title: Ice Cores as Records of Past Climate
text.body:
In the interior of Greenland and Antarctica, the snow that falls each year never fully melts. Instead, it is buried by later snowfall and slowly compressed into solid ice, which in places is more than three kilometres thick. By drilling out long cylinders of this ice, known as cores, scientists obtain an archive of climate stretching back hundreds of thousands of years; the longest continuous record, from Antarctica, covers roughly 800,000 years.

The ice preserves this record in several ways. As snow turns to ice, tiny bubbles of air are sealed inside, giving researchers direct samples of the ancient atmosphere, including its levels of carbon dioxide and methane. The ice itself also carries a temperature signal: the ratio of heavy to light oxygen atoms in the frozen water depends on how cold the air was when the snow fell, with colder conditions leaving less of the heavier form.

Layers of volcanic ash act as fixed time markers, allowing cores drilled at distant sites to be matched with one another. Taken together, these records show that carbon dioxide and temperature have risen and fallen in step through repeated ice ages.

questions.prompt: The phrase "in step" in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to
options: one after the other
in opposite directions
together
unpredictably
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide and temperature 'have risen and fallen in step', meaning they changed together.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred from paragraph 1 about ice from places where much of the snow melts each summer?
options: It would contain more carbon dioxide than polar ice.
It would be thicker than the ice in Antarctica.
It would be easier to drill into than polar ice.
It would give a less complete record of past climate.
questions.explanation: The record depends on snow that 'never fully melts' and builds up year after year, so melting would remove parts of the archive.

questions.prompt: Why does the author discuss heavy and light oxygen atoms in paragraph 2?
options: To explain how air becomes trapped in the ice
To show how the ice reveals past temperatures
To argue that methane levels are hard to measure
To describe how snow is compressed into ice
questions.explanation: The oxygen ratio is introduced as the way the ice 'carries a temperature signal'.

questions.explanation: The passage mentions methane, carbon dioxide and temperature, but never ocean salt content.

They allow cores from distant sites to be matched.
They show where the ice is thickest.
They raise the carbon dioxide level in the ice.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says ash layers act as 'fixed time markers, allowing cores drilled at distant sites to be matched'.

tasks.context: Listen to part of a lecture in a geology class.

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: Today we're looking at how limestone caves form, and the surprising thing is that the main tool is just water. Limestone is made mostly of calcium carbonate, which, um, comes largely from the shells and skeletons of ancient sea creatures. Now, pure water doesn't dissolve limestone very well. But rainwater picks up carbon dioxide from the air, and especially from the soil it trickles through. That turns it into a weak acid, carbonic acid. When this slightly acidic water seeps into cracks in the limestone, it slowly dissolves the rock and carries it away. Over thousands, really hundreds of thousands, of years, small cracks widen into passages, and passages into large chambers. Think of a sugar cube under a dripping tap. The water doesn't smash the cube. It quietly eats away at it, following the weakest paths first. Caves grow the same way, along cracks and layers in the rock. And here's the interesting twist. The same chemistry can work in reverse. When water dripping from a cave ceiling releases its carbon dioxide into the cave air, it can't hold as much dissolved rock. So it leaves tiny deposits of calcite behind. Drop by drop, those deposits build stalactites hanging from the ceiling. So the process that hollows out a cave also decorates it.

options: How slightly acidic water dissolves limestone to form caves

Why limestone caves are found mostly near the ocean
questions.explanation: The professor opens with 'how limestone caves form' and explains how weak carbonic acid dissolves the rock.

From ancient sea creatures
From the soil it passes through
From the air inside caves
questions.explanation: Rainwater picks up carbon dioxide 'especially from the soil it trickles through'.

questions.prompt: Why does the professor mention a sugar cube under a dripping tap?
options: To show that limestone is a very soft rock
To explain how stalactites get their shape
To compare how fast two kinds of rock dissolve
To show how water slowly wears rock along weak paths
questions.explanation: He says the water 'quietly eats away at it, following the weakest paths first', and that caves grow 'the same way'.

options: Caves look more attractive when they are young.
The same chemistry both removes rock and deposits it.
Stalactites form before a cave has been hollowed out.
Visitors often damage the decorations inside caves.
questions.explanation: He calls it 'the same chemistry' working 'in reverse': dissolving rock makes the cave, and depositing calcite builds stalactites.

tasks.context: Listen to part of a lecture in a music history class.

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: So, if you've ever been to an orchestra concert, you'll know that moment before the music starts. The oboe plays one long note, and everyone tunes to it. That note is an A. Today I want to ask two things: why A, and why the oboe? Let's take the oboe first. Its sound is bright and penetrating, so it cuts through the noise of a whole orchestra warming up. And its pitch is fairly fixed. An oboist can't just turn a peg the way a violinist can. So it makes sense for everyone to match the oboe, not the other way round. Now, why A? Look at the string section. Violins, violas, cellos and double basses all have a string tuned to A. So A is the one note every string player can check on an open string, without pressing a finger down at all.

audio.speaker: Student
audio.text: Has A always been the same pitch, though?

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: Not at all. For centuries it varied from place to place, so an A in one city could be noticeably higher than an A in another. That's partly why, in the twentieth century, A at four hundred and forty vibrations per second became the international standard. Even so, some orchestras still tune a little higher, because they feel it gives a more brilliant sound.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
options: How the oboe became part of the orchestra

Why orchestras tune to an A played by the oboe
How the size of a concert hall affects pitch

questions.prompt: Why does the professor point out that all string instruments have an A string?

questions.prompt: What can be inferred about orchestras that tune slightly above 440?

They value a brighter sound over strict uniformity.
questions.explanation: Despite the international standard, they tune higher 'because they feel it gives a more brilliant sound'.

tasks.context: Listen to part of a lecture in an environmental science class.

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: Today I want to talk about composting. Composting is a natural way of turning food scraps and garden waste into rich soil. It's really just a controlled form of rotting. So how does it work? The main workers are tiny living things: bacteria and fungi. They feed on the waste and break it down into smaller and smaller pieces. Earthworms help too. As the bacteria work, they produce heat. In fact, the middle of a good compost pile can get as hot as sixty degrees Celsius. To work well, a compost pile needs four things. Green materials, like vegetable peels and grass. Brown materials, like dry leaves and paper. Water. And air. Let me give you an example. If your pile smells bad, it usually means it's too wet and doesn't have enough air. The easy fix is to add some dry leaves and turn the pile over with a fork. After a few months, you get dark, crumbly compost. Gardeners love it, because it helps plants grow. And it means less rubbish goes to landfill.

How waste is turned into compost

Which animals live in the soil
questions.explanation: The professor explains how composting turns 'food scraps and garden waste into rich soil'.

The dry leaves and paper
The earthworms moving around
Bacteria breaking down the waste

questions.prompt: Why does the professor talk about a pile that smells bad?

To explain why some people do not like compost
To warn students not to make compost at home
To describe how finished compost should smell
questions.explanation: She uses it as an example: a bad smell means the pile is 'too wet and doesn't have enough air'.

She sees it as simple and useful.
She worries that it attracts pests.

tasks.context: Listen to part of a lecture in a psychology class.

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: Let's turn to something marketers have known about for a while, though they don't exactly advertise it: the decoy effect. The idea is that adding a third option, one that almost nobody actually wants, can change which of the other two options people choose. Here's a classic setup. A cinema sells a small popcorn for three dollars and a large for seven. Plenty of people go for the small. Now, add a medium for six fifty. Hardly anyone buys the medium, but suddenly the large looks like a bargain, because for just fifty cents more you get a lot more popcorn. Sales of the large go up. The medium is the decoy. Its job isn't to sell. Its job is to make the large look good. Why does this work? Well, we're not great at judging value in isolation. Is seven dollars a fair price for popcorn? Hard to say. But put it next to six fifty, and the judgement suddenly feels easy. We lean on comparisons because they take so little effort. Now, I'd be careful not to overstate this. In laboratory studies the effect is fairly reliable, but some researchers have found it's weaker in real shopping, where people have more information and more time. So it's a real effect, but it's not quite the marketing magic it's sometimes sold as.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
options: Why cinemas charge high prices for snacks
How shoppers learn to avoid marketing tricks
Why customers usually prefer the cheapest option
How an unattractive option can shift people's choices
questions.explanation: The professor defines the decoy effect as adding an option 'almost nobody actually wants' that changes what people choose.

questions.prompt: According to the professor, why does the decoy effect work?
options: People tend to buy whatever is most popular.
People find it hard to judge value without a comparison.
People always want the largest product available.
People trust prices that end in fifty cents.
questions.explanation: He says 'we're not great at judging value in isolation' and so 'we lean on comparisons'.

questions.prompt: Why does the professor describe the popcorn prices?
options: To illustrate how a decoy makes another option look better
To show that customers usually prefer smaller portions
To explain how cinemas decide on their ticket prices
To contrast laboratory studies with real shopping
questions.explanation: The medium is 'the decoy', and 'Its job is to make the large look good'.

questions.prompt: What is the professor's attitude toward the decoy effect?
options: He doubts that it has ever been shown in studies.
He thinks it explains most consumer decisions.
He accepts it but thinks its power is often exaggerated.
He believes marketers should stop using it.
questions.explanation: He calls it 'a real effect' but warns against overstating it, saying it is 'not quite the marketing magic it's sometimes sold as'.

tasks.context: Listen to part of a lecture in a marine biology class.

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: Last time we talked about light near the ocean's surface. Today we're going down, way down, below about a thousand metres, where sunlight doesn't reach at all. And yet it isn't completely dark down there, because a large share of deep-sea animals make their own light. That's bioluminescence. Chemically, it's fairly simple. A molecule called luciferin reacts with oxygen, helped along by an enzyme, and the reaction releases its energy as light rather than heat. Most of that light is blue, which, not by coincidence, is the colour that travels furthest through seawater. So what's it for? Several things. Take the anglerfish. The female has a glowing lure dangling in front of her mouth. Small fish swim toward the light and, well, that's the last thing they do. So, light as bait.

audio.speaker: Student
audio.text: Couldn't the light also attract predators, though?

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: Good question, and yes, it could. Which is why some animals use light defensively, and quite cleverly. Certain squid and shrimp have light organs on their undersides. Seen from below, their glow matches the faint light coming from above, so their silhouette disappears. It's camouflage made of light, which sounds like a contradiction, but it works.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
options: How sunlight changes colour as it passes through water
How deep-sea animals produce light and what they use it for
Why anglerfish are the most successful deep-sea hunters
How scientists study animals that live in total darkness
questions.explanation: The professor explains the chemistry of bioluminescence and then asks 'what's it for?', giving several uses.

questions.prompt: According to the professor, why is most bioluminescent light blue?
options: Blue light produces the least heat.
Predators are unable to see blue light.
Luciferin itself is a blue molecule.
Blue light travels furthest in seawater.
questions.explanation: She says blue 'is the colour that travels furthest through seawater'.

questions.prompt: Why does the professor mention the anglerfish?
options: To show that only females can produce light
To contrast it with animals near the surface
To give an example of light used to catch prey
To explain how light organs develop over time
questions.explanation: Small fish swim toward its lure and are eaten, which she sums up as 'light as bait'.

questions.prompt: Why does the professor say that 'camouflage made of light' sounds like a contradiction?
options: Light usually makes animals easier to see, not harder.
Squid and shrimp cannot really produce their own light.
Camouflage only works well in shallow, sunny water.
Scientists still disagree about how the light is made.
questions.explanation: Producing light normally attracts attention, as the student's question about predators suggests, yet here it hides the animal's silhouette.

items.prompt: Do you have any brothers or sisters?
items.explanation: Verb + number + adjective + noun: Yes, I have two older brothers. Numbers come before descriptive adjectives.

items.prompt: Is the new gym on campus open yet?
items.explanation: In an indirect question the subject comes before the auxiliary: I'm not sure when it will open (not "when will it open").

items.prompt: What happened to your old laptop?
items.explanation: With a separable phrasal verb, a pronoun object goes between the verb and the particle: I gave it away to my cousin.

items.prompt: Why doesn't your brother drive to school?
items.explanation: The adverb "enough" follows the adjective it modifies: He isn't old enough to drive yet.

items.prompt: How was the new restaurant on Main Street?
items.explanation: "Much" intensifies a comparative and comes before it, and "than" introduces the second item: It was much more expensive than the old one.

items.prompt: Why is the library closed today?
items.explanation: Present continuous passive: subject + is + being + past participle. I heard that the heating system is being repaired.

items.prompt: Who is that woman talking to the manager?
items.explanation: "Whose" is followed directly by the noun it possesses: She's the designer whose plans won the competition.

items.prompt: Did you manage to catch the train to the city?
items.explanation: Past perfect shows the earlier of two past events: No, by the time I got there, it had left.

items.prompt: Was the new scheduling software actually helpful?
items.explanation: After a fronted "Not only", the auxiliary comes before the subject: Not only did it save time, but it also reduced errors.

items.prompt: Why did you turn down the job offer?
items.explanation: An inverted third conditional replaces "if" with "had" before the subject: I would have accepted it had the salary been higher.

tasks.intro: Hi, and thanks for joining me today. I'd like to ask you a few questions about travel and the ways people get around.

questions.text: To start, how do you usually get to school or work, and how long does the trip take?

How is the way people travel today different from when your parents were young? And how do you think it'll change over the next twenty years?
